hooks: Named for Sergei Kirov, the party boss whose 1934 assassination Stalin used as the pretext for the Great Purge.
The city was Vyatka before that, after its river, and there is a long-running campaign to change it back.
Dymkovo toys, brightly painted clay figures made here since the 1400s, are a Russian folk-art standard.
From a Finno-Ugric phrase, probably perä maa, "the far land", which the Russians took as the region's name.
The Permian geological period is named after it — the last period before the dinosaurs, defined from rocks here in 1841.
Kungur ice cave in the region has grottoes that stay frozen year-round.
Named for Yaroslav the Wise, who founded it around 1010 — legend says on the spot where he killed a bear with an axe, which is on the city's arms.
Its centre is a UNESCO site, laid out on a radial plan by Catherine the Great.
Russia's first professional theatre opened here in 1750.
Probably from a Turkic phrase meaning "ten thousand", the size of a Tatar military unit.
The first Russian town in Siberia, founded in 1586 on the site of a Tatar khanate capital.
The oil and gas of the West Siberian basin is administered from here, which makes it one of Russia's richest regions.
From the personal name Ivan — the town grew from a village called Ivanovo.
It was the centre of Russian textiles and is still called the city of brides, because the mills employed mostly women.
The first workers' soviet in Russian history was formed here in 1905, two years before the better-known ones.
From a Finnic river name, Tikhvera; it was Kalinin in Soviet times and changed back in 1990.
Tver was Moscow's main rival for leadership of the Russian lands in the 1300s and lost.
Afanasy Nikitin, a merchant from here, reached India in the 1460s — thirty years before Vasco da Gama — and wrote it up.
Named for the Tom river, from a Ket or Turkic word for a river.
The first university in Siberia opened here in 1888, and it is still the most student-dense city in Russia.
Its wooden lace architecture — carved window surrounds on timber houses — is the best preserved in the country.
"Red ravine" — krasny red, yar a steep bank: the fort was built on a red clay bluff in 1628.
The second largest region in Russia, running 3,000 km from the Arctic to Mongolia.
Norilsk in it is one of the most polluted places in the world from nickel smelting, and one of the northernmost cities anywhere.
From a family name or from kemer, a Turkic word for a riverbank.
The Kuzbass coalfield here produces most of Russia's coal.
Tomskaya Pisanitsa in it has rock carvings up to 4,000 years old on cliffs above the Tom.
From a Bashkir word, possibly selebe, a hollow or pit.
A meteor exploded over the city in 2013 with the force of 500 kilotons, injuring 1,500 people, mostly from flying glass.
Mayak nearby suffered a nuclear accident in 1957 that was kept secret for thirty years and was among the worst ever.
"New Siberian town" — founded in 1893 where the Trans-Siberian Railway crossed the Ob.
It reached a million people faster than any city in history at the time, in under seventy years.
Akademgorodok outside it was built in 1957 as a science city in the forest, and still holds dozens of research institutes.
Named for the Om river, from a Baraba Tatar word meaning "quiet".
It was the capital of White Russia under Admiral Kolchak in 1918–19, and the imperial gold reserve was held here.
Dostoevsky served four years at hard labour in its prison, which became The House of the Dead.
Named for Mikhail Kalinin, a Soviet figurehead — it was Königsberg, "king's mountain", founded by the Teutonic Knights in 1255.
An exclave: it borders Poland and Lithuania and has no land connection to the rest of Russia.
Kant was born, taught and died here and never left the city; his tomb is on the cathedral wall.
Possibly from a word for a cut or a slope, or from the Erzya people.
Old Ryazan was destroyed by the Mongols in 1237 and never rebuilt; the modern city is a different town that took the name.
Yesenin, one of Russia's best-loved poets, was born in a village here.
Named for Lenin, whose real surname was Ulyanov and who was born here when it was Simbirsk.
Kerensky, the head of the Provisional Government Lenin overthrew, was born in the same town, and his father taught Lenin.
It sits on the Volga, and its bridge is among the longest in Europe at nearly 6 km.
Possibly from a word for a hidden or sheltered place.
It has made Russian weapons since 1712 and its samovars since the 1770s — "taking a samovar to Tula" is the Russian coals to Newcastle.
Tolstoy's estate Yasnaya Polyana is here, where he wrote War and Peace and is buried under a mound with no headstone.
From debryansk, "place of thickets" — debri means dense forest.
Its forests sheltered the largest Soviet partisan movement of the war, tens of thousands of fighters behind German lines.
It was the most heavily contaminated Russian region after Chernobyl, which is over the border in Ukraine.
From the Samara river, possibly from a Turkic or Iranian word for steppe river.
It was Kuybyshev in Soviet times and was the reserve capital in 1941: a bunker was dug for Stalin 37 m down, and he never used it.
The Zhiguli hills force the Volga into a great loop here, and Soviet rockets including Gagarin's were built in the city.
From the river, probably a Finno-Ugric name.
Meyerhold, the theatre director shot in 1940, was born here, and his house is a museum.
It sits on the forest-steppe border, and its black earth is some of the most fertile in Russia.
From lipa, the lime tree, which grew along its river.
Peter the Great built ironworks here to arm his new navy, and the town grew around them.
It has one of the largest steel plants in Russia and one of the country's oldest spa waters.
Named for the Irkut river, from a Buryat word.
Lake Baikal is here: the deepest lake in the world at 1,642 m, holding about a fifth of all unfrozen fresh water on earth.
Exiled Decembrist officers settled in the city after 1825 and turned a frontier town into "the Paris of Siberia".
"Fortress on the Or" — though the town was moved and now sits on the Ural, not the Or.
Its knitted goat-down shawls are so fine that a full-size one passes through a wedding ring.
It was the gateway to Central Asia for the Russian Empire, and the first Soviet space launches were tracked from here.
From the river Kur, itself probably from a word for a bird or a spring.
The 1943 battle here was the largest tank battle ever fought and ended German offensive capacity in the east.
The Kursk Magnetic Anomaly beneath it is the largest iron ore deposit in the world, and it deflects compass needles.
Of uncertain origin — possibly from a personal name or from voron, a raven.
Peter the Great built Russia's first navy here in 1695–96, on a river far from any sea, and sailed it down to the Don.
Its black earth is among the most fertile soil on earth; a cube of it was displayed at the 1900 Paris Exposition as a standard.
Probably from Turkic sary tau, "yellow mountain", for the hills above the Volga.
Gagarin landed in a field in this region in 1961 and was found by a farmer and her granddaughter, who thought he was an alien.
Chernyshevsky, whose novel What Is to Be Done? shaped a generation of revolutionaries, was born here.
"Volga town" — it was Tsaritsyn, then Stalingrad, then renamed in 1961 during de-Stalinisation.
The battle here in 1942–43 was the bloodiest in history, with perhaps two million casualties, and turned the war.
The Motherland Calls statue on Mamayev Kurgan was the tallest in the world when built, at 85 m with the sword.
Named for Yerofey Khabarov, a seventeenth-century explorer whose treatment of the Amur peoples was brutal enough that Moscow recalled him.
The city sits on the Amur, directly across from China, and the river freezes solid enough to drive on.
The region is the size of Germany and Poland together, with 1.3 million people.
Rostov-on-Don, named to distinguish it from the older Rostov Veliky near Moscow; the name is from a personal name, Rost.
It is the capital of the Don Cossacks, whose self-governing host held the steppe frontier for the tsars.
Sholokhov's And Quiet Flows the Don, which won the Nobel Prize, is set in its villages.
Probably from Hajji Tarkhan, a title meaning a privileged man who had made the pilgrimage.
It sits on the Volga delta, the largest in Europe, where the river fans into 500 channels before the Caspian.
Most of the world's beluga caviar came from here before the sturgeon collapsed; it is now farmed.
Greek for "city of the cross", from a cross found when the fortress was built in 1777.
Gorbachev was born and made his career here before Moscow.
Its mineral water spas — Kislovodsk, Pyatigorsk, Yessentuki — have drawn Russians since the 1800s, and Lermontov was killed in a duel at Pyatigorsk.
"Gift of the reds" — renamed in 1920 from Yekaterinodar, "Catherine's gift", for the land she gave the Cossacks.
Sochi in it hosted the 2014 Winter Olympics in a subtropical resort where palms grow.
It is Russia's main agricultural region, growing most of its rice, tea and wine.
